content: Good morning. I know we talked last week mostly about the equipment and the renovation timeline, but this week I've been almost entirely focused on suppliers. I finally feel like the dry goods side is locked in, and I've also got a really promising produce arrangement in place that came together in a way I didn't expect. The kitchen flooring is still going in — they ran into a subfloor issue that pushed things back by about four days — and the equipment from the Italian vendor is clearing customs early next week, so that's all still on track. But I wanted to use today's session to walk you through the sourcing decisions in detail, because a few of them involve cost structures I want your read on, and there's one relationship that came together through an introduction that I think is worth explaining the context of.

Good morning, Kenta. A four-day flooring delay is frustrating but not the kind of thing that typically cascades badly unless it pushes you into a chain of dependencies — I assume you've flagged it with the contractor to understand what it means for the handover date? But yes, let's spend this session on suppliers. Dry goods and produce are foundational for the kind of kitchen you're running. Northern Italian cooking at a serious level is honest in a way that leaves nowhere to hide — the quality of your olive oil, your flour, your seasonal vegetables reads directly on the plate in a way it simply doesn't in cuisines that involve longer cooking or heavier seasoning. Getting those supply relationships right before you open is one of the highest-leverage things you can do. Tell me what you've sorted out.

The contractor says the four-day delay doesn't affect the equipment installation schedule because those were already separated by a buffer week for exactly this kind of thing. So we're still tracking to the original handover. Good. Okay, so let me start with olive oil because that was actually the most research-intensive of the sourcing decisions and I think it's the one with the most interesting backstory in terms of how the Japanese import market for premium Italian oils actually works. I knew from the beginning of planning this restaurant that I wanted to be using Tuscan oil — specifically from the Frantoio cultivar tradition, which has a flavor profile that's very characteristic of central Italian cooking and fits northern Italian finishing applications really well. Peppery, grassy, bitter at the finish, high in polyphenols, which you want because they indicate freshness and they have flavor significance on the plate. The problem is the Japanese import landscape for high-end Italian oils is quite fragmented. Most of the large-volume importers are focused on Spanish or Greek oils because those move in bigger quantities and the logistics are more straightforward. Premium Tuscan oils are a smaller niche. I spent about three weeks contacting various importers before I connected with a company called Solleone Japan, which is an importer that focuses specifically on premium Italian oils. They're not generalists — Italian oil is their whole business — and that specialization shows up in things like cold-chain management, vintage tracking, and the depth of producer relationships they maintain.

Solleone Japan is a name I've heard associated with the premium Italian import niche in Japan, and your read on them sounds right — importer specialization matters enormously for premium olive oil because the product is so susceptible to handling failures that generalist importers introduce without even realizing it. Heat exposure during transit, improper storage before distribution, inadequate stock rotation — all of these are problems that a focused importer is structured to avoid and a generalist often isn't. The Frantoio cultivar focus makes a lot of sense for a northern Italian kitchen. It's worth noting that a lot of Tuscan oils marketed internationally are Frantoio-dominant blends rather than single-varietal, but the flavor direction is consistent — that peppery, slightly bitter, grassy profile you're describing is very different from the buttery, round character of Ligurian oils or the more neutral Spanish styles. For a northern Italian kitchen, especially if you're doing anything with crudo, raw preparations, or light pastas where the oil is a primary flavor carrier, that peppery intensity is exactly what you want. What producer specifically did they connect you with?

The producer is Frantoio Franci — that's the brand and the producer name, they're the same entity. They're based in the Maremma hills in southern Tuscany, which is a slightly warmer microclimate than the classic Chianti or Siena zones but it produces oils with great intensity and a very clean extraction character. Frantoio Franci has won awards at Flos Olei — that's probably the most respected Italian olive oil guide — and they're known for cold extraction, single-estate sourcing, and excellent traceability on their harvest and pressing dates. Which, for a restaurant, matters a lot because you want to know you're working with oil from the most recent harvest and not something that's been sitting in a warehouse for eighteen months. Solleone Japan imports Frantoio Franci with full lot documentation, so I can trace each delivery to a specific pressing date. The price is 4,200 yen per 500ml bottle, which is at the higher end of what I was expecting but not unreasonable for a single-estate Tuscan oil with that level of documentation and traceability. I'm going to use this oil specifically as a finishing oil and for dressing raw preparations — not for cooking, not for bulk applications. So the volume I'm going through is meaningful but controlled.

Frantoio Franci is an excellent producer — that Flos Olei recognition is meaningful because the guide is genuinely rigorous and the competition in the premium Italian oil category is fierce. The Maremma appellation sometimes flies under the radar compared to the classic Chianti Classico zone, but it's producing some of the most consistent high-polyphenol oils in Tuscany. At 4,200 yen per 500ml, you're in a price tier that's fully defensible as a cost input for a restaurant at the level you're targeting in Higashi-Azabu. If you're using one and a half to two bottles per week on average, that's roughly 25,000 to 34,000 yen per month on finishing oil — meaningful but not extravagant for a dinner-only operation. How is Solleone Japan handling delivery and minimum orders? And did you ask about what happens in a harvest year where the Frantoio Franci quality isn't up to their usual standard?

I asked exactly that question about vintage variation, and it was actually one of the things that sold me on the relationship. Olive oil quality varies year to year similarly to wine — drought years, excessive heat during flowering, irregular rainfall, disease pressure — all of these affect the final oil character and sometimes the polyphenol levels significantly. Solleone Japan told me they send tasting samples from each new harvest before they ask restaurant clients to commit to a seasonal order, so if in a given year the Frantoio Franci quality doesn't meet my standard, I'm not stuck with inventory. They maintain relationships with two or three backup Tuscan producers for exactly that reason, so the supply chain doesn't break even if I need to switch in a given season. On the delivery side, the minimum order is six bottles per delivery, which is perfectly calibrated to my usage — six bottles is roughly three weeks of inventory, so I'm ordering approximately every three weeks. They operate a Tokyo delivery route twice a month, and for restaurant clients in the 23 wards they do direct delivery. The detail I was most pleased about is that they use a climate-controlled vehicle for summer deliveries — they told me they maintain below 20 degrees Celsius in transit even in July and August in Tokyo. That's critical. An oil like Frantoio Franci that you're paying 4,200 yen per 500ml for should not be riding around in an uninsulated delivery van in 35-degree heat.

The climate-controlled transit detail is exactly the right thing to have pressed them on, and the fact that they proactively maintain below 20 degrees in summer is a meaningful operational commitment. A lot of importers who sell you on premium positioning then put the product in a van that reaches ambient temperature in July, and you lose a significant fraction of the oil's character before it even arrives at your kitchen. The vintage flexibility policy also tells you something important about how Solleone Japan thinks about their restaurant relationships — they're not trying to lock you into quantity commitments and move product regardless of quality; they're structured around keeping the restaurant satisfied, which is what you want in a long-term supplier. The six-bottle minimum per delivery fitting naturally into your usage rhythm is also a good sign that they've structured their minimum orders around realistic restaurant consumption patterns rather than their own logistics convenience. Now let me ask about flour, because for a northern Italian kitchen doing fresh pasta daily, your flour sourcing is just as consequential as your oil. Have you worked that out?

Flour was actually more straightforward than the oil search, in retrospect, because the answer was obvious from the start — for fresh pasta at a serious Italian restaurant you use Caputo 00, full stop. Caputo is the Naples mill, they've been milling specialty flours for over a century, and the 00 designation for pasta specifically is calibrated for the protein content and granularity you need to get proper gluten development in fresh pasta without overworking the dough. I've used Caputo in other kitchen contexts and I wasn't going to experiment with a Japanese domestic substitute or a different Italian brand when Caputo is the established standard. The question was which importer to use, and after a few conversations I went with Suzuki Foods. They're a mid-sized food importer based in Osaka with a Tokyo distribution hub in Koto-ku. They're not a single-category specialist the way Solleone Japan is, but they have a strong Italian pantry dry goods division — pasta, flour, specialty ingredients — and they've been importing Caputo specifically for about fifteen years, which means their supply chain and quality management for that product line is mature. The pricing they quoted me is 3,800 yen per 25kg sack, which I benchmarked against a reference from a chef colleague of mine who runs a Neapolitan pizza operation in Shibuya and was paying 4,100 yen per 25kg sack through a different importer for the same product. So I feel confident that the Suzuki Foods pricing is genuinely competitive.

Caputo 00 is the correct answer for fresh pasta and I'd agree that experimenting with alternatives when you have a proven standard available introduces unnecessary risk, especially in the pre-opening period when you're trying to stabilize your kitchen processes rather than troubleshoot flour variables. The 300-yen-per-sack difference between your price at 3,800 yen per 25kg sack and what your colleague is paying at 4,100 is meaningful at volume — if you're going through one sack every ten to fourteen days, that's a saving of somewhere between 600 and 900 yen per month, which isn't transformative but it's real money for the same product. Koto-ku is a reasonable location for a Tokyo distribution hub serving central Tokyo restaurants, it's a standard freight corridor and the logistics to Higashi-Azabu are workable. Did you ask Suzuki Foods about delivery frequency and minimum order quantities, and did you check into their lot documentation practices? With flour, especially 00 for daily pasta production, you want to know you're working with product that was milled recently, not flour that's been sitting in a warehouse since the previous season.

Yes, I pushed them on both points. On delivery frequency, Suzuki Foods runs a delivery schedule to central Tokyo three times a week — Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays — and the account rep confirmed that same-week orders are accommodated as long as I place the order by noon the day before the delivery. That level of flexibility is important for a small restaurant operation where I don't want to be carrying more than three weeks of inventory at a time. The minimum order is two sacks per delivery, which fits my usage. At my anticipated pasta output for a dinner service of 30 to 40 covers, I estimate going through roughly one sack of Caputo 00 every ten to fourteen days, so two sacks per order gives me approximately three to four weeks of inventory. I have a dedicated dry goods room in the basement that the renovation included specifically for this kind of storage — temperature controlled, properly shelved, designed to keep flour in optimal condition. On lot documentation, I did ask specifically, and this was a slightly more involved conversation because initially the account rep was giving me best-before dates, which aren't what I want. I want milling dates. I explained that for fresh pasta production where you're working with the flour every day, the milling date tells you much more than a best-before — it tells you how far into the shelf life you are and whether the hydration behavior you calibrated at the beginning of the month is still going to hold as the batch ages. They came back to me after checking with their operations team and confirmed they can provide milling date documentation on request for each lot. I'll be asking for that every delivery.

Pushing for milling dates rather than best-before dates is exactly the right ask — it tells you how far into the shelf life you are and whether your hydration calibration will hold as the batch ages. The fact that Suzuki Foods could accommodate it after checking internally suggests the data exists; they just don't surface it proactively. Tuesday-Thursday-Saturday delivery with a same-day noon cutoff gives you real operational flexibility. Between the Caputo 00 from Suzuki Foods and the Frantoio Franci from Solleone Japan, your dry pantry backbone is solid. Now tell me about produce — I have a feeling that's where the story gets more interesting.

Yes, the produce story is the most interesting one. I have to start with the origin of the connection, because it's one of those things where the value of a trusted network reveals itself in unexpected ways. You know I've been working with my accountant, Hiroshi Tanabe — he's been handling all the financial structure for this project, we've talked about him in previous sessions. I didn't know until about six weeks ago that Tanabe's wife runs a catering business. It came up completely offhand in a call where we were reviewing the equipment budget — he mentioned that she had recently switched her produce sourcing contact for her catering business and her ingredient costs for Italian-style vegetables had dropped noticeably while the quality had gone up. I asked him what had changed, and he said she'd started working with a produce broker who specializes in European-style vegetables for Western cuisine restaurants. I asked him if he could make an introduction, and he was happy to — he actually seemed pleased that a contact through his wife's business world might be useful to me. He introduced me to a man named Kenji Ueno, who operates as a produce broker out of a firm called Ueno Seika. Ueno Seika works specifically with Tsukiji-Ota Market — that's the main wholesale produce market that absorbed the trading relationships and many of the vendors from the original Tsukiji inner market after the move to Toyosu — and Kenji Ueno is specifically known among his restaurant clients for sourcing European-style vegetables and specialty Italian produce items that don't flow easily through general wholesale channels.

That connection is a good illustration of why the professional network around a project matters beyond its obvious functions. Tanabe is there to manage your accounting, but a good accountant who's been close to a project often makes lateral connections instinctively. His wife's catering business having a prior working relationship with Kenji Ueno at Ueno Seika gives you a real-world operational reference — she's been placing orders, receiving produce, dealing with the day-to-day reality of working with him. That's far more meaningful than anything from a cold introduction. The specialization in Tsukiji-Ota Market is also significant: after the Tsukiji move, that market became the real center of gravity for specialty produce in Tokyo, and a broker with deep relationships there is in a completely different position from someone working through general wholesale channels. What was your first meeting with Kenji Ueno like, and how did you structure the arrangement?

The first meeting was very good. We met in person at a coffee place in Tsukishima, which is geographically close to the market area — he'd been at Tsukiji-Ota Market from around three AM that morning and Tsukishima was convenient. He's in his mid-fifties, calm, very direct, with the kind of unhurried confidence that you see in people who are genuinely expert in their domain and don't feel any need to sell themselves. Within about ten minutes of talking, he was describing which farms in Nagano are currently growing radicchio this season, which prefecture is producing the best cavolo nero right now, what the supply situation on cardoons looks like for autumn — all of this from memory, no notes, with the specificity of someone who is in daily contact with these supply chains. That kind of market knowledge is not something you can fake and it's not something you get from a product catalog. It comes from twenty-plus years of being at the market every morning and building relationships with every layer of the supply chain. The arrangement we settled on is spec-based sourcing. I provide him with a seasonal produce list at the start of each month — the kinds of items I'm planning to work with, the quantities I anticipate, the quality thresholds I need. For a northern Italian kitchen that means things like radicchio, cavolo nero, castelfranco, treviso, fennel, cardoons when they're available in autumn, different varieties of winter squash, fresh peas in spring, and so on. He sources to those specs, but he also proactively contacts me when something exceptional comes through Tsukiji-Ota Market that he thinks I'd want to know about — a particularly beautiful batch of something seasonal, or a small quantity of something unusual that he knows fits my menu direction. That proactive intelligence function is, honestly, probably the most valuable part of the arrangement.

The way you're describing Kenji Ueno matches what you want in a produce broker at this level. The best brokers at Tsukiji-Ota Market are market people who happen to also sell to restaurants — the relationship dynamic is somewhat reversed from a typical supplier interaction. The spec-based structure with proactive intelligence is exactly the right framework for a northern Italian kitchen. Radicchio, castelfranco, treviso, cavolo nero, cardoons — these are items that a generalist Tokyo supplier either won't carry or will carry past their peak. Having a broker at Tsukiji-Ota Market every morning sourcing to your specification is what makes those varieties viable as consistent menu elements rather than lucky-day specials. What's the pricing structure, and how does delivery work in practice?

The pricing structure is a broker margin on top of market rate, which is standard for this kind of arrangement — Kenji Ueno is not a wholesaler, he's a broker, so he's not marking up on an inventory he holds; he's charging a margin for the sourcing service and the quality filtering he applies at the market. I've done some benchmarking on a few test items — comparing what he quoted me against the general wholesale prices I could find from publicly available references for those product categories — and his margin is in the range of 8 to 12 percent above the market rate depending on the item. For the sourcing service he provides, and particularly for the quality filtering and specialty expertise, I think that's very fair. Some items where he's doing more active sourcing work might be at the higher end of that range, more commodified items might be closer to 8 percent. I'm comfortable with the overall cost structure. On delivery: Ueno Seika operates a small refrigerated van, and for restaurant clients in central Tokyo, Kenji Ueno does a morning delivery run himself. The schedule for Higashi-Azabu would put my delivery as the second or third stop on his Minato-ku route, arriving somewhere between five-thirty and seven AM. That timing is ideal for a dinner-only kitchen — the produce arrives right at the beginning of kitchen prep, which means by the time my team is doing the detailed prep work for evening service, everything is already on site and has been inspected. I place the order by eight PM the evening before, he's at Tsukiji-Ota Market from around three AM, sources what I need, and delivers by mid-morning at the latest. The lead time is as tight as it can possibly be while still going through the market sourcing step. And he's agreed to send me a weekly text briefing on Sunday evenings — a short summary of what looks exceptional for the coming week and what's likely to be scarce or priced high due to weather, seasonal pressures, or supply disruptions. That forward intelligence on the market is very useful for menu planning.

Eight to twelve percent over market rate for a specialist produce broker with Kenji Ueno's depth of market access and the sourcing service he provides is very reasonable — you're paying for daily expertise, quality filtering, and relationship access, not just a logistics markup, and the alternative of sourcing that category of specialty Italian vegetables yourself through general wholesale channels would either cost more, deliver lower quality, or both. The five-thirty to seven AM delivery to Higashi-Azabu fitting naturally into his existing Minato-ku route is logistically clean — you're not paying a premium for an out-of-the-way detour, and the timing is perfectly matched to a dinner-only kitchen's prep schedule. The eight PM order cutoff the evening before is a tight cadence but it becomes natural once your team has rhythm, and the benefit is that you're receiving produce purchased at market that same morning rather than something redistributed from a warehouse. The Sunday evening market briefing is worth calling out specifically — that weekly forward read on scarcity and exceptional product is the kind of intelligence that lets you write your weekly menu with real market awareness rather than working backwards from what you were able to get. It's a qualitatively different way of planning a menu. I want to ask about one more dimension: how are you thinking about formalizing these three supplier relationships? You have Solleone Japan, Suzuki Foods, and Ueno Seika — are any of these on written contracts, and have you thought about what level of documentation makes sense for each one given how differently they're structured?

Good question, and this is actually something I've been thinking about in the context of Tanabe's role specifically. Since Tanabe is my accountant and he's tracking all of the business expenditures for this project, he has a legitimate professional interest in understanding the supplier arrangements at some level of detail. And since it was Tanabe who introduced me to Ueno through his wife's catering connection, he has a bit of a different relationship to that particular supplier arrangement than he does to the others — there's a personal network element there that makes it feel right to loop him in more deliberately. For the Solleone Japan and Suzuki Foods relationships, those are both operating under standard vendor purchase order terms — their standard business terms, nothing bespoke. I've reviewed both sets of terms and they're clean. No unusual exclusivity clauses, no onerous liability provisions, standard delivery and payment terms. Those relationships are well-structured from a contractual standpoint and don't require anything special. The Ueno Seika arrangement is where I want to be more thoughtful, because the nature of produce brokering means you can't have a rigid contract — you can't fix pricing in advance on perishables, you can't guarantee quantity commitments when you're sourcing to market availability. But I do want a written memo of understanding that documents the terms of the relationship in a reference form: the broker margin range, the delivery timing and logistics, the Sunday briefing arrangement, the spec-based ordering process, minimum order parameters, and the general quality standards I've communicated to him. I'll ask Tanabe to review whatever we put together, partly because he knows Ueno through his wife's business and can give me a reality check on whether the terms I'm documenting reflect what the actual experience of working with Ueno Seika is like.

That's a well-calibrated approach across the three relationships. Standard vendor terms for Solleone Japan and Suzuki Foods makes sense — those are straightforward buyer-supplier arrangements where the supplier's own terms are adequate. The memo of understanding for Ueno Seika is the right call: it documents mutual expectations without trying to impose rigid contractual structure on what is inherently a market-flexible brokering relationship. Involving Tanabe in reviewing the Ueno Seika documentation is sound for multiple reasons — as your accountant he should have visibility into a recurring cost relationship that affects food cost, and his connection to Kenji Ueno through his wife's catering business gives him a practical benchmark. Whatever you document — the margin range, delivery arrangement, Sunday briefing — he can cross-reference against what she's actually experienced, which is a genuine verification rather than just a formality. Between the Frantoio Franci through Solleone Japan, the Caputo 00 through Suzuki Foods, and the specialty produce through Ueno Seika at Tsukiji-Ota Market, you've built a supply foundation that's well above average for a new opening.
